rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. “Duolingo says beta users talked to its AI character for nine minutes at a stretch” is a clean, provable data angle; B’s “Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence” invents causality from two adjacent facts and hopes nobody asks for the bridge. A is press strategy; B is half strategy, half TED-talk posture in a blazer.
gaps_in_A: “Critics called Duolingo shallow. Its answer is a video call with an AI character.” The angle is strong, but “its answer” slightly overstates intent; the update does not say Duolingo framed the feature as a response to critics.
“The next earnings report is the natural follow-up moment.” Reasonable inference for a public company, but it is not in the update and should stay framed as a reporting follow-up, not a peg.
“Duolingo, the language app, is now teaching chess” is usable but thin launch coverage unless the course scope, curriculum owner, or user reach can be nailed down.
gaps_in_B: “whether Duolingo is pivoting from language app to AI learning platform” overreads one chess course and one AI conversation feature. That is a thesis looking for an executive quote, not a grounded angle yet.
“whether it can replace a human tutor” invents a competitive/displacement frame the update never supplies. Conversation practice is not automatically tutor replacement.
“Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence” is the worst kind of confident: maybe true, completely unproven here.

“uses two supplied facts (nine-minute sessions, 40% growth) as the counter-evidence” repeats the exact fallacy it later refuses. Time spent and DAU growth do not answer whether gamification is shallow learning.
